newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cereol plants may process gene-soybeans - Eridania.
newsitem.headline: Cereol plants may process gene-soybeans - Eridania.

text.p: Eridania Beghin-Say said on Friday that its European plants that already crush and refine imported U.S. soybeans were likely to process the new genetically modified soybeans.
It was virtually impossible to differentiate between the two crops, the company said.

"Regarding crushings and refinings activity, the plants of the Cereol group that process soybeans imported from the U.S. cannot differentiate between the products processed," a company spokesman said in reply to a Reuters query.

The European Union (EU) approved in March the sale of soybeans imported from the U.S. which have been genetically modified to resist a weed killer in a technique developed by the chemicals company Mansanto Co
Europe is due for its first shipments of the new beans later this year when the new U.S. harvest comes in.
About two percent of the new 1996 U.S. crop contains the so-called transgenic soybeans.
The products have been declared safe by health authorities in the United States, Europe, Japan, Canada and Argentina.
But environmentalist group Greenpeace has staged an international campaign against the news beans, saying allergic reactions could not be ruled out.
EuroCommerce, a large European trade group has asked for labelling of the so-called transgenic soybeans so consumers can tell what is in their food.
But the grain industry says it would be costly and impractical to try to separate the crops that are indistinguishable from traditional varieties.
On Thursday a German unit of Unilever decided not sell products containing edible oils made from the modified genes in response to consumer concern.
But Unilever said this had not changed the company's overall stance on the issue, saying it regarded the beans as safe.
Eridania Beghin-Say also produces and markets edible oils made from protein-rich soybeans.
In Italy the Giglio Oro brand makes soyoil from refined soybeans it purchases on world markets.
In France Lesieur does the same but the soyoil produced is destined only for exports.
Both Giglio Oro and Lesieur plan to continue buying their refined soybeans on the market, the spokesman said.
In France Lesieur also markets ISIO 4, an edible oil that combines several seeds, including soybeans.
In a new and unrelated development Lesieur decided a few months ago to replace the soyoil component of ISIO 4 by rapeoil.
The decision was taken after internal research showed the switch would improve the nutritional quality of ISIO 4, the spokesman said.
-- Dominique Vidalon, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5432
